cues.text: A Schism Eighteen Years Old
Hippolytus , a learned Roman priest and one of the most productive theological writers of his generation, had broken communion with the Roman Church nearly two decades earlier.
He objected first to Pope Zephyrinus's Christology, then to Pope Callistus I's willingness to readmit grave sinners to communion after penance.
Hippolytus set himself up as a rival bishop — often regarded as the Church's first antipope — and continued in open schism through the reigns of Callistus's next two successors.
Pope Pontian
Pontian became bishop of Rome on July 21, 230, and during his pontificate presided over a Roman synod that concurred with a council at Alexandria in condemning certain teachings of Origen.
Through Pontian's five-year reign, the schism of Hippolytus persisted, a running wound in the young Roman Church even as it faced no organized imperial persecution.
Arrest and Exile

In 235, the Emperor Maximinus Thrax launched a persecution aimed chiefly at Christian leaders, and Pontian was among its first targets, arrested and condemned to the notoriously brutal mines of Sardinia .
Hippolytus was seized and exiled to the same island.
Rather than leave the Roman see vacant while unable to govern from exile, Pontian took the unprecedented step of resigning the papacy on September 28, 235.
He was the first pope in history known to have done so, clearing the way for a successor to be elected in Rome.
Reconciliation in the Mines
Sometime shortly before or after Pontian's resignation, the two old rivals reconciled.
Confined together in the same harsh Sardinian exile, Hippolytus renounced his schism and returned to communion with the legitimate Roman Church, closing a rift that had lasted some eighteen years.
Both men died in Sardinia not long after, worn down, ancient sources say, by the deliberate cruelty of their confinement.
Return to Rome
Pope St. Fabian later arranged for the remains of both men to be brought back to Rome and buried with honor on the same day, August 13.
Pontian was laid in the papal crypt of the Catacomb of Callistus, and Hippolytus, fittingly reconciled at last, nearby on the Via Tiburtina.
An epigram composed by Pope Damasus for Hippolytus's tomb records that he urged his own followers, before his death, to return to the Catholic Church.
Legacy

The joint feast of Pontian and Hippolytus stands as one of the earliest and most striking examples in Church history of reconciliation triumphing over years of bitter theological division, sealed in the shared suffering of persecution and martyrdom.
Hippolytus's own theological and liturgical writings, despite his years in schism, remain valued sources for understanding the early Roman Church's worship and doctrine.
